title: What is a shotgun house?
summary: Josh and Chuck explore the shotgun house, a long, narrow, single-file American vernacular house. They cover its supposed name origin (a gun fired through the front door exiting the back, which they call a probably untrue story), its features (narrow lots, high ceilings, front-to-back aligned doors, gingerbread trim, front porches built off the ground), and its roots in West Africa (the Yoruba "to gun"/"showgun"), spread to Haiti, and arrival in New Orleans after the Haitian Revolution. They discuss property tax rules based on frontage and rooms in New Orleans, the camelback variant, the first print use of the term in the Atlanta Journal-Constitution in 1903, and kit houses sold for about a hundred dollars. They describe its spread to Atlanta neighborhoods, Chicago, and southern Oklahoma, its role as a social front-porch community space, its decline in the 1920s, use in disaster housing after the 1906 San Francisco earthquake, and pop culture ties (John Mellencamp's "Pink Houses," Elvis Presley's and Aaron Neville's childhood homes). They also mention the tiny house movement. The episode closes with listener mail from a listener who met the Beastie Boys in Las Vegas in 1987 as a fifteen-year-old, and a request for listener house stories.

segments.title: Opening banter and David Byrne reference
segments.summary: Josh and Chuck open the show and banter about the David Byrne lyric about living in a shotgun shack, and introduce the topic of Atlanta and shotgun houses.

segments.title: Hurricane Katrina and why shotgun houses matter
segments.summary: The hosts recall worry about losing shotgun houses after Hurricane Katrina, note they are found across the US, and say New Orleans is where they were born in the US and African American contributions to the architecture.

segments.title: Physical features of shotgun houses
segments.summary: Shotgun houses are long and narrow, often close to neighboring houses, with high ceilings, few early indoor plumbing, and aligned interior doors. The hosts discuss the popular but probably untrue story that a shotgun could be fired through the house.

segments.title: Architectural flourishes and African roots
segments.summary: Gingerbread trim and carved brackets adorned these houses. The hosts trace the design to Haiti and further to West Africa, where Yoruba-language names 'to gun' and 'showgun' are linked to the name.

segments.title: Property taxes, camelbacks and early print use
segments.summary: New Orleans property taxes were based on frontage, later including rooms, and shotgun houses avoided extra rooms. Camelback variants added a rear second story. The term appeared in the Atlanta Journal-Constitution in 1903 in a rent ad, and kit houses cost about a hundred dollars.

segments.title: Haitian Revolution and migration to New Orleans
segments.summary: The hosts explain that the Haitian Revolution led by Toussaint Louverture drove out white plantation owners and that refugees brought the shotgun house style to New Orleans, a diverse city at the time.

segments.title: Spread to Atlanta, Chicago and Oklahoma
segments.summary: Shotgun houses spread beyond New Orleans to working-class African American neighborhoods such as Chicago and Atlanta areas, and to southern Oklahoma, where all-black towns and runaway slaves integrated with Native American tribes.

segments.title: Front porch culture and legacy
segments.summary: Chuck explains the front porch as a community gathering space, its link to later American porches, stoops and wraparound porches, and the elevated porch in New Orleans.

segments.title: Decline, disaster housing, pop culture and tiny houses
segments.summary: Shotgun houses waned in the 1920s, were used as cheap housing after the 1906 San Francisco earthquake and as prefabricated labor housing, and appear in songs and in Elvis Presley's and Aaron Neville's childhood homes. The tiny house movement is noted as a modern revival.

segments.title: Listener mail: Beastie Boys encounter
segments.summary: A listener describes meeting the Beastie Boys on their 1987 tour in Las Vegas as a fifteen-year-old, and the hosts invite listeners to share stories about interesting homes.
